title: Data structures
description: Purpose, guarantees, costs and use-case recognition for each structure, independent of a particular pattern.

nodes.name: Array
nodes.description: Contiguous storage: O(1) random access, O(n) insert/delete by shifting; doubles as a direct-address table for bounded values.

facets.recognize: Uses an array as a frequency/visited table when values are bounded (e.g. 1..n) instead of a hashmap.
facets.explain: States access/insert/delete costs and why middle insertion is O(n).
facets.implement: Reads, writes and shifts elements correctly.

misconceptions.desc: Assumed inserting or deleting in the middle is O(1).
Used a hashmap when values are bounded and a plain array would be simpler and faster.

nodes.name: Sorted array properties
nodes.description: Monotonic order: duplicates are adjacent, pairs can be found with converging pointers, two sorted arrays merge linearly.

facets.recognize: Notices sorted input and exploits it (two pointers, merge, adjacent duplicates, binary search).
facets.explain: States which properties sortedness guarantees and what sorting destroys (original indices).

misconceptions.desc: Ignored that input is sorted; used hashing or nested loops instead of a linear pass.
Sorted the input when original indices are part of the answer (e.g. Two Sum returning indices).

nodes.name: Matrix (2D grid)
nodes.description: Rows, columns, diagonals, layers/boundaries; square vs rectangular; properties like transpose symmetry.

facets.recognize: Identifies the structure an algorithm needs: layers, boundaries, transpose, first row/column as storage.
facets.explain: Knows how a transpose or row reversal moves each (i, j).
facets.implement: Traverses by row, column, diagonal and boundary.

misconceptions.desc: Assumed a square matrix where m != n is allowed.

nodes.name: Hash map
nodes.description: Key -> value lookup in O(1) average; used for frequency counts and value -> index lookup.

facets.recognize: Reaches for a hashmap for counting, value -> index lookup or 'seen before?' with unbounded values; also knows when O(1) space beats it.
facets.explain: States the trade: O(n) extra space for O(1) average lookup.
facets.implement: Designs the key/value pair that answers the question (value -> index vs value -> count).

misconceptions.desc: Stored the wrong mapping (index -> value instead of value -> index).
Used a hashmap where O(1) extra space is achievable (Boyer-Moore, XOR, math, two pointers).

nodes.name: Hash set
nodes.description: Membership and de-duplication in O(1) average.

facets.recognize: Uses a set for membership or dedupe, and knows when duplicates must be counted instead.

misconceptions.desc: Used a set where the count of duplicates matters.

nodes.name: String as a character sequence
nodes.description: A string is an array of characters: scans, two pointers and counting arrays all apply, and a 26- or 256-slot array counts characters.

facets.recognize: Reaches for a fixed-size counting array for characters and treats strings with array techniques.
facets.explain: Knows the cost of indexing (O(1)) versus substring, comparison and concatenation (O(length)).
facets.implement: Iterates, compares and builds strings correctly.

misconceptions.desc: Assumed only lowercase letters; broke on uppercase, digits, spaces or other characters.
Used a hashmap for character counts where a fixed array of 26 or 256 is simpler and faster.
Treated substr, comparison or concatenation as O(1).

nodes.name: Singly linked list
nodes.description: Nodes joined by next pointers: O(1) insert or delete at a known node, O(n) to reach a position, no random access.

facets.recognize: Solves list problems by relinking, without copying values into an array.
facets.explain: States the costs: O(n) access by position, O(1) relink at a known node.
facets.implement: Traverses, inserts and deletes at the head, middle and tail without losing nodes or following nullptr.
facets.trace: Draws the pointers before and after each relink.

misconceptions.desc: Did not handle inserting or deleting at the head, or an empty or one-node list.
Stopped the walk one node too early or too late (while (curr) versus while (curr->next)).
Copied the list into an array to solve it, using O(n) space where O(1) was expected.
Assumed reaching the kth node is O(1).

nodes.name: Doubly linked list
nodes.description: Each node links to both neighbours, so a node can be removed in O(1) given only a pointer to it; every relink updates two pointers.

facets.explain: Explains why prev pointers make O(1) removal possible (used by LRU caches).
facets.implement: Updates next and prev on both sides, including the head's prev and the tail's next.
facets.trace: Draws next and prev after each change.

misconceptions.desc: Updated next but not prev (or the reverse), leaving a half-linked node.
Left the new head's prev or the new tail's next pointing at a removed node.
While reversing, swapped prev and next but then advanced with the wrong pointer.

nodes.name: Stack (last in, first out)
nodes.description: Push and pop at one end in O(1); the top is always the most recent unfinished item.

facets.recognize: Reaches for a stack when the most recent unfinished item decides what happens next (brackets, undo, nearest greater).
facets.explain: Explains LIFO order and O(1) push and pop.
facets.implement: Uses and builds stacks with empty checks.

misconceptions.desc: Popped or read the top without checking that the stack is empty.
Used a queue or a rescan where last-in-first-out order is what the problem needs.
Did not check that the stack is empty at the end (unmatched items remain).

nodes.name: Queue and deque (first in, first out)
nodes.description: Push at the back and pop at the front in O(1); a deque allows both ends. Queues drive BFS and sliding windows.

facets.recognize: Reaches for a queue when items must be handled in arrival order (BFS levels, streams).
facets.explain: Explains FIFO order and how a circular array or two stacks implement it.
facets.implement: Implements a circular-array queue and uses deque ends correctly.

misconceptions.desc: In an array queue, did not wrap front or rear with % capacity, or confused full with empty.
Removed from the wrong end of a deque.
Used q.size() in a loop condition while pushing, instead of saving the size first.

nodes.name: Heap / priority queue
nodes.description: Gives the smallest (or largest) item in O(1) and inserts or removes in O(log n).

facets.recognize: Uses a heap when the next item to process is always the minimum or maximum (Dijkstra, top k, merging streams).
facets.explain: States O(log n) push/pop and that priorities cannot be changed in place.
facets.implement: Builds a min-heap with greater<> and skips stale entries instead of updating them.

misconceptions.desc: Assumed a priority_queue entry can be updated in place; push a new entry and skip stale ones instead.
Re-sorted the whole collection after every insert instead of using a heap.
Built a max-heap where a min-heap was needed (or the reverse).

nodes.name: Binary tree
nodes.description: Each node has up to two children; almost every tree problem is recursion on the left and right subtrees with nullptr as the base case.

facets.recognize: Frames tree questions as 'what do I need from each subtree?'.
facets.explain: Uses height, depth, levels, leaves and complete/full/perfect correctly.
facets.implement: Defines TreeNode and writes recursion with a nullptr base case.
facets.trace: Can trace recursive calls and returns on a small tree.

misconceptions.desc: Followed root->left or root->right without a nullptr check, or had no base case for an empty tree.
Mixed up height (down to the deepest leaf) and depth (down from the root), or counted edges where nodes were asked.
Assumed values are ordered like a BST in a plain binary tree.
Mixed up full, complete, perfect and balanced trees.

nodes.name: Binary search tree
nodes.description: Everything in the left subtree is smaller and everything in the right subtree larger than the node; search, insert and delete take O(h).

facets.recognize: Uses the ordering to visit one root-to-leaf path instead of the whole tree.
facets.explain: States that the property holds for whole subtrees, not just children, and that h can be n when unbalanced.
facets.implement: Searches and inserts iteratively or recursively using comparisons.

misconceptions.desc: Believes checking each node against its two children is enough for the BST property.
Searched the whole tree (O(n)) instead of following the ordering (O(h)).
Assumed O(log n) operations without a balanced tree; a skewed BST is O(n).

nodes.name: Graph (adjacency list)
nodes.description: Vertices joined by edges, directed or not, weighted or not; usually stored as an adjacency list using O(V + E) space.

facets.recognize: Spots graphs hidden in grids, word transformations, dependencies and equations.
facets.explain: Compares adjacency list and matrix costs, directed and undirected edges, and vertex numbering.
facets.implement: Builds the adjacency list from the input, both directions for undirected edges, sized for the vertex numbering.

misconceptions.desc: Added an undirected edge in one direction only.
Sized the adjacency list n when vertices are numbered 1..n (or the reverse).
Used an adjacency matrix (O(V²)) for a large sparse graph.
Traversed only from vertex 0, missing other components.

nodes.name: Disjoint set union (union-find)
nodes.description: Tracks which component each element is in; with path compression and union by rank or size, find and union are near O(1).

facets.explain: Explains why path compression and union by rank keep the trees shallow.
facets.implement: Writes find with path compression and unions roots by rank or size.

misconceptions.desc: Did not compress paths or union by rank or size, so find degraded to O(n).
Linked the elements themselves instead of their roots.
Did not check whether two elements were already connected before uniting or counting.
Compared parent[a] == parent[b] instead of find(a) == find(b).
